title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
summary: Chapter 10 'Light - Reflection and Refraction' explains the behavior of light when it interacts with different surfaces. It covers the laws of reflection, image formation by plane and spherical mirrors, the concept of refraction, lens types, and image formation by lenses. The chapter also discusses the power of lenses and the human eye as a natural optical instrument. Students learn about the sign conventions for spherical mirrors and lenses, the mirror and lens formulas, and magnification. The chapter concludes with defects of vision and their correction using lenses.
hotTopics: Refraction through a rectangular glass slab

sections.heading: Reflection of Light
sections.para: Reflection is the phenomenon of bouncing back of light rays into the same medium after striking a surface. The laws of reflection state that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane. For a plane mirror, the image formed is virtual, erect, of the same size as the object, and laterally inverted. The image is formed behind the mirror at the same distance as the object is in front of it. Spherical mirrors can be concave or convex. Concave mirrors converge light rays and can form both real and virtual images depending on the object position.
points: Reflection occurs when light bounces back from a surface.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Plane mirrors produce virtual, erect images of the same size.
Concave mirrors converge light rays and can form real or virtual images.
Convex mirrors diverge light rays and always form virtual, diminished images.
The focal length of a spherical mirror is half its radius of curvature.

keyTerms.meaning: Bouncing back of light rays into the same medium
An imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence
The angle between the incident ray and the normal
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal
A spherical mirror with reflecting surface curved inwards
A spherical mirror with reflecting surface curved outwards

sections.trick: Remember 'RI' for Reflection - Incident angle equals Reflection angle.
sections.examPointer: CBSE frequently asks questions on ray diagrams for plane and spherical mirrors, mirror formula (1/f = 1/v + 1/u), and magnification (m = v/u). Expect 2-3 mark questions on these concepts.

sections.heading: Spherical Mirror Formula
sections.para: The mirror formula relates the object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f) of a spherical mirror. It is expressed as 1/f = 1/v + 1/u. According to the Cartesian sign convention, distances measured in the direction of incident light are positive, and those opposite are negative. For concave mirrors, the focal length is negative, while for convex mirrors, it is positive. Magnification (m) is given by m = v/u, where positive magnification indicates an erect image and negative indicates an inverted image. The mirror formula and magnification can be used to determine the position, nature, and size of the image formed by a spherical mirror.
points: The mirror formula is 1/f = 1/v + 1/u.
Sign convention: Distances in the direction of incident light are positive.
For concave mirrors, focal length is negative.
For convex mirrors, focal length is positive.
Magnification m = v/u, where positive m means erect image.
The formula works for both concave and convex mirrors with proper sign convention.

keyTerms.meaning: Distance of the object from the pole of the mirror
Distance of the image from the pole of the mirror
Distance of the principal focus from the pole of the mirror
Ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object
Set of rules to assign positive or negative values to distances

sections.trick: Remember 'CUN' for Concave mirror sign convention: Centre of curvature, focal point, and pole are all on the same side as incident light, so they're negative.
sections.examPointer: Numerical problems on mirror formula and magnification are common. Expect 3-5 mark questions requiring application of sign conventions and solving for unknown values. Practice ray diagrams alongside calculations.

sections.heading: Refraction of Light
sections.para: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another due to change in speed. The laws of refraction state that the incident ray, refracted ray, and normal all lie in the same plane, and the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant for a given pair of media. This constant is called the refractive index (n) of the second medium with respect to the first. When light enters a denser medium, it bends towards the normal, and when it enters a rarer medium, it bends away from the normal. The refractive index of a medium is also equal to the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in that medium.
points: Refraction occurs due to change in speed of light when passing between media.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
When light enters a denser medium, it bends towards the normal.
When light enters a rarer medium, it bends away from the normal.
Refractive index n = sin(i)/sin(r) = c/v.
The refractive index of air is approximately 1.0.

keyTerms.meaning: Bending of light as it passes from one medium to another
The angle between the incident ray and the normal
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal
Ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium
The ratio of sines of angles of incidence and refraction is constant

sections.trick: Remember 'DRAN' for refraction: Denser medium, Ray bends towards Normal; Rarer medium, Ray bends away from Normal.
sections.examPointer: Questions on refraction through a rectangular glass slab are common. Expect 2-3 mark questions on calculating refractive index, angle of refraction, and lateral displacement. Diagrams are essential.

sections.heading: Refraction Through Spherical Lenses
sections.para: Spherical lenses are transparent optical instruments with at least one spherical surface. They can be convex (converging) or concave (diverging). Convex lenses are thicker in the middle and converge light rays, while concave lenses are thinner in the middle and diverge light rays. The principal axis passes through the centers of curvature of the lens surfaces. The optical center is a point on the principal axis where light passes without deviation. The principal focus is a point where parallel rays converge after refraction (for convex lenses) or appear to diverge from (for concave lenses). The focal length is the distance between the optical center and the principal focus. A lens has two foci, one on each side.
points: Convex lenses converge light rays and are thicker in the middle.
Concave lenses diverge light rays and are thinner in the middle.
The optical center is a point where light passes undeviated.
The principal focus is where parallel rays converge or appear to diverge from.
A lens has two foci, one on each side.
The focal length is half the radius of curvature for a thin lens.

keyTerms.meaning: A lens that converges light rays, thicker in the middle
A lens that diverges light rays, thinner in the middle
A point on the principal axis where light passes undeviated
Point where parallel rays converge or appear to diverge from
Distance between optical center and principal focus

sections.trick: Remember 'CT' for Convex lens: Converges light, forms both real and virtual images.
sections.examPointer: Ray diagrams for image formation by convex and concave lenses are frequently asked. Expect 3-4 mark questions on lens formula, magnification, and nature of images formed in different positions.

sections.heading: Lens Formula and Magnification
sections.para: The lens formula relates the object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f) of a lens. It is expressed as 1/f = 1/v - 1/u. According to the Cartesian sign convention, for convex lenses, focal length is positive, and for concave lenses, it is negative. Magnification (m) is given by m = v/u, where positive magnification indicates an erect image and negative indicates an inverted image. The lens formula can be used to determine the position, nature, and size of the image formed by a lens. When the object is placed at infinity, the image is formed at the focus. When the object is placed at 2F, the image is also formed at 2F, same size, and inverted.
points: The lens formula is 1/f = 1/v - 1/u.
For convex lenses, focal length is positive.
For concave lenses, focal length is negative.
Magnification m = v/u, where positive m means erect image.
When object is at infinity, image forms at focus.
When object is at 2F, image forms at 2F, same size, inverted.

keyTerms.meaning: Distance of the object from the optical center of the lens
Distance of the image from the optical center of the lens
Distance of the principal focus from the optical center
Ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object
Reciprocal of focal length in meters, measured in dioptres

sections.trick: Remember 'LV' for Lens formula: Lens formula has a minus sign (1/f = 1/v - 1/u), unlike mirror formula which has plus (1/f = 1/v + 1/u).
sections.examPointer: Numerical problems on lens formula and magnification are very common. Expect 3-5 mark questions requiring application of sign conventions and solving for unknown values. Practice ray diagrams alongside calculations.

sections.heading: Power of Lens
sections.para: The power of a lens is a measure of its ability to converge or diverge light rays. It is defined as the reciprocal of the focal length in meters and is measured in dioptres (D). For convex lenses, power is positive as they converge light, while for concave lenses, power is negative as they diverge light. When multiple lenses are in contact, the combined power is the algebraic sum of individual powers. The power of a lens can be calculated using the formula P = 1/f, where f is the focal length in meters. A lens with a shorter focal length has more power, as it can converge or diverge light more strongly.
points: Power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in meters.
Power is measured in dioptres (D).
Convex lenses have positive power as they converge light.
Concave lenses have negative power as they diverge light.
Combined power of lenses in contact is the algebraic sum of individual powers.
A lens with shorter focal length has more power.

keyTerms.meaning: Reciprocal of focal length in meters, measured in dioptres
Unit of power of lens, equal to reciprocal of focal length in meters
A lens that converges light rays, has positive power
A lens that diverges light rays, has negative power
Algebraic sum of powers of lenses in contact

sections.trick: Remember 'PD' for Power of lens: Positive for Diverging concave lens? No, Positive for Converging convex lens, Negative for Diverging concave lens.
sections.examPointer: Questions on calculating power of lenses and combined power are common. Expect 2-3 mark numerical problems using P = 1/f. Remember to convert focal length to meters before calculation.

sections.heading: Human Eye
sections.para: The human eye is a natural optical instrument that forms an image on the retina. The eye has a convex lens system that focuses light on the retina, where light-sensitive cells detect the image. The pupil controls the amount of light entering the eye, and the ciliary muscles change the curvature of the lens to focus on objects at different distances. The ability of the eye to focus on near and far objects is called accommodation. The least distance of distinct vision is the minimum distance at which an object can be seen clearly, which is approximately 25 cm for a normal eye. The far point is the maximum distance at which an object can be seen clearly, which is infinity for a normal eye.
points: The human eye forms images on the retina.
The pupil controls the amount of light entering the eye.
Ciliary muscles change the lens curvature for focusing.
Accommodation is the ability to focus on near and far objects.
Least distance of distinct vision is about 25 cm for normal eye.
Far point is infinity for a normal eye.

keyTerms.meaning: Light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye where images are formed
Opening in the iris that controls light entering the eye
Muscles that change the curvature of the lens
Ability of the eye to focus on objects at different distances
Minimum distance at which an object can be seen clearly

sections.trick: Remember 'PCL' for eye parts: Pupil, Ciliary muscles, Lens work together for focusing.
sections.examPointer: Questions on the structure and working of the human eye are common. Expect 2-3 mark questions on accommodation, near point, far point, and the role of different parts of the eye.

sections.heading: Defects of Vision and Their Correction
sections.para: The common defects of vision are myopia, hypermetropia, and presbyopia. Myopia, or near-sightedness, is a condition where a person can see near objects clearly but distant objects appear blurred. This occurs when the eye lens converges light rays to a point in front of the retina. It is corrected using a concave lens of appropriate power. Hypermetropia, or far-sightedness, is a condition where a person can see distant objects clearly but near objects appear blurred. This occurs when the eye lens converges light rays to a point behind the retina. It is corrected using a convex lens. Presbyopia is the loss of accommodation due to aging, corrected by using bifocal lenses with both concave and convex parts.
points: Myopia is near-sightedness, corrected by concave lenses.
Hypermetropia is far-sightedness, corrected by convex lenses.
Presbyopia is loss of accommodation due to aging.
In myopia, image forms in front of the retina.
In hypermetropia, image forms behind the retina.
Bifocal lenses correct presbyopia.

keyTerms.meaning: Near-sightedness, corrected by concave lenses
Far-sightedness, corrected by convex lenses
Loss of accommodation due to aging, corrected by bifocal lenses
Diverging lens used to correct myopia
Converging lens used to correct hypermetropia

sections.trick: Remember 'MC' for Myopia Correction: Myopia needs Concave lens.
sections.examPointer: Questions on defects of vision and their correction are very common. Expect 3-4 mark questions explaining the causes and corrections of myopia, hypermetropia, and presbyopia with ray diagrams.

sections.heading: Prism and Dispersion of Light
sections.para: A prism is a transparent optical element with flat, polished surfaces that refract light. When white light passes through a prism, it splits into its constituent colors, a phenomenon called dispersion. This occurs because different colors of light have different wavelengths and thus different refractive indices in the prism material. Red light has the longest wavelength and least deviation, while violet light has the shortest wavelength and maximum deviation. The band of colors formed is called a spectrum. The splitting of light into its constituent colors is due to the variation in refractive index with wavelength, known as dispersion. The angle between the emergent rays of red and violet light is called the angle of dispersion.
points: A prism refracts light and splits it into constituent colors.
Dispersion occurs due to different refractive indices for different colors.
Red light has least deviation, violet has maximum deviation.
The band of colors formed is called a spectrum.
Dispersion is due to variation in refractive index with wavelength.
The angle between red and violet emergent rays is angle of dispersion.

keyTerms.meaning: Transparent optical element with flat surfaces that refract light
Splitting of light into its constituent colors
Band of colors formed due to dispersion of light
Ratio of speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium
Angle between emergent rays of red and violet light

sections.trick: Remember 'RV' for colors in dispersion: Red is first, Violet is last in the spectrum.
sections.examPointer: Questions on dispersion of light through a prism are common. Expect 2-3 mark questions on why dispersion occurs, the order of colors in the spectrum, and the concept of angle of deviation.

sections.heading: Atmospheric Refraction
sections.para: Atmospheric refraction is the bending of light rays as they pass through the layers of the Earth's atmosphere with varying densities. This phenomenon causes several optical effects, including the apparent flattening of the Sun at sunrise and sunset, the twinkling of stars, and the advanced sunrise and delayed sunset. The apparent position of an object in the sky is higher than its actual position due to atmospheric refraction. This is because light rays from the object bend towards the normal as they enter the denser layers of the atmosphere. The twinkling of stars occurs because the atmospheric conditions change continuously, causing the apparent position and brightness of the star to fluctuate.
points: Atmospheric refraction is due to varying densities of air layers.
It causes apparent flattening of the Sun at sunrise/sunset.
Stars twinkle due to atmospheric refraction.
The apparent position of celestial objects is higher than actual.
Light bends towards normal as it enters denser air layers.
Advanced sunrise and delayed sunset are due to atmospheric refraction.

keyTerms.meaning: Bending of light due to varying densities of air layers
Apparent change in brightness and position of stars due to atmospheric refraction
Observed position of an object, different from actual position due to refraction
Sun appears before it actually rises due to atmospheric refraction
Sun appears after it actually sets due to atmospheric refraction

sections.trick: Remember 'AT' for Atmospheric refraction effects: Apparent position is higher, Twinkling of stars.
sections.examPointer: Questions on atmospheric refraction effects are common. Expect 2-3 mark questions explaining why stars twinkle, why the Sun appears flattened at sunrise/sunset, and why sunrise is advanced and sunset is delayed.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of a redox reaction?
mcqs.explanation: In the reaction 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, hydrogen is oxidized and oxygen is reduced, making it a redox reaction.

mcqs.question: What is the pH of a neutral solution at 25°C?
mcqs.explanation: A neutral solution has a pH of 7 at 25°C, as it contains equal concentrations of H+ and OH- ions.

mcqs.question: Which compound is commonly known as baking soda?
mcqs.explanation: Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) is commonly known as baking soda and is used in cooking and baking.

mcqs.question: What is the chemical formula of washing soda?
mcqs.explanation: Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate with the formula Na2CO3·10H2O.

mcqs.question: Which metal is extracted by the electrolytic refining method?
mcqs.explanation: Copper is extracted and purified by electrolytic refining, where impure copper is used as an anode.

mcqs.question: What is the function of thermite reaction?
options: To extract iron from its ore
mcqs.explanation: The thermite reaction is highly exothermic and is used for welding railway tracks and other metal parts.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is an amphoteric oxide?
mcqs.explanation: Aluminum oxide (Al2O3) is amphoteric, meaning it can react with both acids and bases.

mcqs.question: What is the chemical name of plaster of Paris?
mcqs.explanation: Plaster of Paris is calcium sulfate hemihydrate with the formula CaSO4·0.5H2O.

mcqs.question: Which process is responsible for rancidity of fats?
mcqs.explanation: Rancidity is caused by the oxidation of fats and oils, leading to unpleasant odors and flavors.

mcqs.question: What is the chemical formula of ethanol?
mcqs.explanation: Ethanol has the molecular formula C2H5OH and is commonly found in alcoholic beverages.

mcqs.question: Which hormone is secreted by the pancreas to regulate blood sugar?
mcqs.explanation: Insulin is secreted by the pancreas and helps lower blood sugar levels by promoting glucose uptake.

mcqs.question: What is the function of xylem in plants?
mcqs.explanation: Xylem is responsible for transporting water and minerals from roots to other parts of the plant.

mcqs.question: Which part of the brain controls balance and posture?
mcqs.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movements and maintains balance and posture.

mcqs.question: What is the chemical reaction involved in esterification?
mcqs.explanation: Esterification is the reaction between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid to form an ester and water.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a homologous series?
mcqs.explanation: Alkanes, alkenes, and alkynes are all homologous series with similar chemical properties and gradual changes in physical properties.

mcqs.question: What is the main function of nephrons in the kidneys?
mcqs.explanation: Nephrons are the functional units of the kidneys that filter blood and produce urine.

mcqs.question: Which type of pollination involves transfer of pollen from one flower to another of the same plant?
mcqs.explanation: Geitonogamy is the transfer of pollen from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower on the same plant.

mcqs.question: What is the chemical formula of ethanoic acid?
mcqs.explanation: Ethanoic acid, commonly known as acetic acid, has the formula CH3COOH.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a non-biodegradable pollutant?
mcqs.explanation: Plastic is a non-biodegradable pollutant that persists in the environment for a long time.

mcqs.question: What is the role of hemoglobin in blood?
mcqs.explanation: Hemoglobin in red blood cells binds to oxygen in the lungs and transports it to tissues.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the process of corrosion and describe two methods to prevent iron from rusting.
boardQuestions.answer: Corrosion is the gradual destruction of metals by chemical reactions with their environment, such as oxidation when iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form rust (iron oxide). Two methods to prevent iron from rusting are: 1) Galvanization: Coating iron with a layer of zinc, which acts as a sacrificial anode and prevents oxygen from reaching the iron. 2) Painting: Applying a protective layer of paint on the iron surface to prevent contact with oxygen and moisture, thus inhibiting the rusting process.

boardQuestions.question: Write the chemical equations for the reactions involved in the preparation of bleaching powder and explain its uses.
boardQuestions.answer: Bleaching powder is prepared by passing chlorine gas over slaked lime (calcium hydroxide). The chemical reaction is: Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 -> CaOCl2 + H2O. Bleaching powder has several uses: 1) It is used as a bleaching agent for textiles, paper, and wood pulp. 2) It is used for disinfecting water supplies and swimming pools. 3) It is used in the manufacture of chloroform and other organic compounds. 4) It acts as an oxidizing agent in various chemical reactions.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the process of electrolytic refining of copper with a labeled diagram.
boardQuestions.answer: Electrolytic refining of copper is a process used to purify impure copper. The setup consists of an electrolyte containing copper sulfate (CuSO4) solution. A thick block of impure copper is made the anode, and a thin strip of pure copper is made the cathode. When electric current is passed, copper atoms from the impure anode lose electrons and dissolve into the solution as Cu2+ ions: Cu (impure) -> Cu2+ + 2e-. These Cu2+ ions then move to the cathode where they gain electrons and deposit as pure copper: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu (pure). Impurities like gold and silver settle below the anode as anode mud. This process yields highly pure copper (99.99%) suitable for electrical applications.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the structure and function of the human heart with a labeled diagram.
boardQuestions.answer: The human heart is a muscular organ about the size of a fist located in the chest cavity between the lungs. It has four chambers: two atria (upper chambers) and two ventricles (lower chambers). The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava, which then flows to the right ventricle. The right ventricle pumps this blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery for oxygenation. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary veins, which then flows to the left ventricle. The left ventricle pumps this oxygenated blood to the rest of the body through the aorta. The heart has four valves: tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, and aortic, which ensure unidirectional blood flow. The heart's rhythmic contractions (heartbeat) are controlled by electrical impulses generated by the sinoatrial node (SA node), making it an efficient pump that circulates blood throughout the body.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the process of photosynthesis and write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction.
boardQuestions.answer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and some other organisms use sunlight to synthesize foods from carbon dioxide and water, generally involving the green pigment chlorophyll and generating oxygen as a byproduct. The process occurs in the chloroplasts of plant cells. The balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis is: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. This equation shows that six molecules of carbon dioxide and six molecules of water, in the presence of light energy and chlorophyll, produce one molecule of glucose and six molecules of oxygen.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the structure and function of a neuron with a labeled diagram.
boardQuestions.answer: A neuron is the basic unit of the nervous system and consists of three main parts: the cell body (soma), dendrites, and axon. The cell body contains the nucleus and cytoplasm and is responsible for maintaining the life of the cell. Dendrites are branched extensions that receive signals from other neurons and transmit them toward the cell body. The axon is a long, thin extension that carries nerve impulses away from the cell body to other neurons, muscles, or glands. The axon is often surrounded by a myelin sheath that insulates it and speeds up impulse transmission. Neurons transmit electrical impulses called action potentials, which allow for communication within the nervous system.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the process of double fertilization in flowering plants with a labeled diagram.
boardQuestions.answer: Double fertilization is a unique process in flowering plants where two fertilization events occur in the embryo sac. It begins with the pollen grain landing on the stigma and growing a pollen tube down through the style to the ovary. The pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and reaches the embryo sac. One male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form the zygote, which develops into the embryo. The second male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the primary endosperm nucleus, which develops into the endosperm that provides nutrition to the embryo. This process ensures that the embryo has both genetic material from the parents and a food supply for its development. The result is the formation of a seed containing an embryo and endosperm, surrounded by the seed coat.

boardQuestions.question: Calculate the resistance of a conductor if a current of 0.5 A flows through it when a potential difference of 12 V is applied across its ends.
boardQuestions.answer: To calculate the resistance of the conductor, we use Ohm's law: V = I × R, where V is the potential difference, I is the current, and R is the resistance. Given V = 12 V and I = 0.5 A, we can rearrange the formula to find R: R = V / I. Substituting the given values: R = 12 V / 0.5 A = 24 Ω. Therefore, the resistance of the conductor is 24 ohms.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the differences between soaps and detergents.
boardQuestions.answer: Soaps and detergents are both cleaning agents but have some key differences: 1) Chemical composition: Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of fatty acids (e.g., sodium stearate), while detergents are sodium salts of sulfonic acids (e.g., sodium lauryl sulfate). 2) Action in hard water: Soaps form insoluble precipitates (scum) with calcium and magnesium ions in hard water, reducing their effectiveness. Detergents do not form such precipitates and work well in hard water. 3) Biodegradability: Soaps are generally biodegradable, while some synthetic detergents are not and can cause environmental pollution. 4) Cleaning action: Both soaps and detergents have hydrophilic and hydrophobic parts that help remove dirt by forming micelles, but detergents are generally more effective in a wider range of conditions.
